When we release, we first upload every new asset under a new versioned name, then update the manifest so it points to those names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never points at a file that isn't there yet. If we switched first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the upload finished would request missing assets and get a broken page. Uploading first means that by the time any browser can see the new manifest, everything it references already exists.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. Those pages will still request the old versioned names, for example when they lazy-load a script or image later. If we deleted the old files, those requests would fail and the open pages would break. Keeping them lets those browsers finish on the old version while new visitors get the new one.

Our release happens in two steps: upload, then switch.

**Upload first.** Every new asset (JS bundles, CSS, images) goes up under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2e.js`, alongside the existing files. Nothing points to these files yet, so uploading them changes nothing for users. They are just sitting there, ready.

**Then switch the manifest.** The manifest is the single file that tells browsers which asset names to load. Once every new asset is confirmed uploaded, we update the manifest to reference the new names. That one change is the actual release.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest switch is only safe if everything it points to already exists. If we switched first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the uploads finished would request files that aren't there yet and get 404s: broken scripts, missing styles, a half-rendered page. Uploading first means that the moment the new manifest is visible, every file it names is already available. It also makes the switch cheap to undo: rolling back is just pointing the manifest at the previous names again.

**Why we keep the old assets:** releases don't reach every browser at the same moment. Someone who loaded the page a minute before the switch is still running the old manifest, and their page will keep requesting old asset names as they navigate, lazy-load a chunk, or pull in a stylesheet. If we deleted the old files at release time, those users would hit 404s mid-session. Caches (CDN edges, browser caches, service workers) can also hold the old manifest for a while. Keeping the old assets lets those sessions finish cleanly, and it keeps rollback instant because the previous version's files are still in place.

Versioned names are what make both steps work: since old and new files never share a name, they can coexist without one overwriting the other, and caches never serve a stale file under a current name.

A release has two steps: first we upload every new asset under a new versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never points at a file that isn't there yet. Once the manifest switches, browsers immediately start requesting the new names. If any of those files were still missing, those browsers would get broken pages. Uploading everything first means the switch only exposes files that already exist.

Each release has two steps: upload the new assets, then switch the manifest. The manifest is the only thing that decides which version users get, so switching it is the moment the release goes live.

**Upload first, then switch.** Every new asset has a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`. Uploading it doesn't affect anyone, because nothing references that name yet. Once every new file is in place, we switch the manifest, and every name it points to already exists. If we switched first, browsers would load the new manifest, request files that aren't there yet, and get 404s: missing scripts, unstyled pages, or a broken app until the upload finished. Uploading first makes the release a single cutover with no half-deployed state.

**Keep the old assets.** The switch doesn't reach browsers that already loaded the previous manifest. Open tabs, cached HTML, and CDN edges still hold the old manifest and keep requesting the old names. This matters most for files fetched later in a session, such as lazy-loaded code chunks, images, and fonts loaded on navigation. If we deleted the old files, those users would hit 404s in the middle of a session, even though they did nothing wrong. Keeping the old files lets every client finish on the version it started with.

The old assets also make rollback fast. Switching the manifest back to the previous names restores the last release instantly, with no re-upload, because those files never went away.
